results.name: alt_btc_residual_catchup
results.one_liner: When ETH/SOL has lagged its BTC-implied 24h move by 2+ sigma in the direction BTC moved, trade the alt to close the gap.
results.why: Alts are priced off BTC plus noise, so a large beta-adjusted gap after a BTC move is usually temporary flow in the alt. The loser is whoever pushed the alt away from BTC with a large one-off order.
results.risk: Single leg, not a hedged pair: the result is mostly BTC direction. A gap can also be real news about the alt.

results.name: asia_range_london_breakout
results.one_liner: First hourly close outside the 00:00-07:00 UTC range during 07:00-10:59 UTC: go with it for up to 8 hours.
results.why: Europe brings the first real volume of the day into a range set in thin Asian hours, and stops cluster just outside that range. The losers are overnight range traders and their stops.
results.risk: Crypto trades 24/7, so the session edge may be folklore borrowed from FX; false breaks are frequent.

results.name: bollinger_mean_reversion
results.one_liner: In a choppy market (low efficiency ratio), fade the first close outside the 2-sigma band back to the 20-bar mean.
results.why: Without a trend, excursions beyond two sigma are mostly liquidity-driven noise that market makers are paid to absorb. The losers are breakout traders who buy the top and sell the bottom of a range.
results.risk: The one excursion that is a real breakout costs several average wins; the chop filter switches off late.

results.name: breakout_retest
results.one_liner: After a volume-backed break of the 72-hour range, bid passively at the broken level and trade the retest.
results.why: Traders who missed the break and those trapped on the wrong side both want to deal at the old range edge, which turns resistance into support. The losers are late chasers shaken out on the retest.
results.risk: Adverse selection: the limit fills exactly when the breakout is failing, and the best breakouts never come back.

results.name: btc_breakout_alt_lag
results.one_liner: BTC closes outside its 48-hour range while ETH/SOL is still inside its own: take the alt in BTC's direction to its range edge.
results.why: BTC is the price-discovery leader and alt order books reprice after it. The losers are alt market makers and passive orders still quoting stale levels.
results.risk: At 1h resolution most of the lag is already arbitraged; what is left may be the alt being weak for a reason.

results.name: btc_shock_alt_lag
results.one_liner: BTC prints a 2+ ATR hourly bar and ETH/SOL moved less than half as much in ATR terms: take the alt in BTC's direction for 3 bars.
results.why: Under-reaction: the alt has not finished repricing a BTC shock by the end of the hour. The losers are liquidity providers in the alt who have not yet moved their quotes.
results.risk: Rare, and alts normally over-react to BTC shocks; an alt that did not move may be pinned by a large resting order.

results.name: donchian_trend
results.one_liner: Go with a close beyond the 55-bar channel, leave on a close through the opposite 20-bar channel, 2-ATR stop.
results.why: Large crypto moves arrive as multi-day trends because big holders build and unload slowly and leveraged traders are forced to chase. The losers are range faders and under-margined counter-trend positions that must be closed into the move.
results.risk: Whipsaw: most breakouts fail, so it bleeds small losses plus fees until a real trend pays for them.

results.name: funding_crowd_unwind
results.one_liner: When 3-day funding is in the top decile and price closes below the 72-hour low, short the unwind (mirror for crowded shorts).
results.why: A crowded, levered side has to cut once price moves against it, and its exits push price further. The losers are leveraged longs (or shorts) who paid up to hold and are now offside.
results.risk: The trigger bar is often the capitulation itself, so the entry is late; overlaps with plain breakdown selling.

results.name: funding_extreme_fade
results.one_liner: When 3-day funding is in the top/bottom 5% of the last 90 days and beyond a floor, trade against the paying side for up to 3 days.
results.why: Extreme funding means one side is crowded and paying heavily to stay; the carry bleeds them and any adverse move forces exits. The losers are late leveraged traders on the paying side, and the fade also collects the funding.
results.risk: Funding can stay extreme for weeks in a strong trend; with no price trigger this stands in front of the move.

results.name: liq_flush_reclaim
results.one_liner: After a liquidation flush, wait up to 6 bars for an up bar that closes above the prior bar's high, then buy with a stop under the flush low.
results.why: Same forced-selling logic as the plain flush trade, but it waits for proof that the sellers are done. The losers are late shorts who sold the flush low and now have to cover.
results.risk: Confirmation gives away part of the bounce, and in a real downtrend the reclaim bar is only a pause.

results.name: liq_flush_retest_bid
results.one_liner: After a liquidation flush, rest a bid at the flush low for 12 bars; target the middle of the flush bar.
results.why: A second visit to a liquidation low meets less forced supply than the first, and the passive buyer earns the maker fee. The losers are breakdown sellers hitting a low that has already been cleared of stops.
results.risk: The order only fills if price comes back down, i.e. after the first bounce has already failed.

results.name: liq_flush_reversal
results.one_liner: After a 1h bar that falls 2+ ATR on 3x volume with open interest down 2%+, buy the next open for a half retrace.
results.why: A liquidation cascade is forced selling at any price, and once the forced flow ends there is an air pocket above. The losers are the liquidated longs; the winner is whoever supplies them liquidity.
results.risk: Flushes come in series: the first is often not the last, and the stop sits under a low that is easily taken.

results.name: london_open_fakeout_fade
results.one_liner: A 07:00/08:00 UTC bar pokes outside the Asian range but closes back inside: fade it toward the middle of the range.
results.why: The start of a new session often runs the obvious stops beyond the overnight range before the real direction is set. The losers are breakout traders who entered on the poke.
results.risk: Small targets next to costs, and a wick on a 1h bar is a crude proxy for a stop-run.

results.name: ma_trend_atr_stop
results.one_liner: Long while the 20-bar average is above the 100-bar average, short below; flip on the cross, 3-ATR disaster stop.
results.why: Positions that fight a persistent move are closed over days, not minutes, so direction persists. The losers are traders who fade a trend early and anyone forced out by margin.
results.risk: Late in and late out; a sideways market produces a string of crosses that each lose a little.

results.name: negative_funding_uptrend
results.one_liner: Long when 24h funding is negative while price is above its 50-bar average and up on the day; out when funding turns positive or price loses the average.
results.why: Shorts are paying to hold a position the tape is not rewarding, which makes them fuel for the next leg up. The losers are those shorts; the long is paid to wait.
results.risk: Negative funding with a firm price can also be spot selling hedged in perps: informed flow, not trapped shorts.

results.name: ny_open_drive
results.one_liner: If 13:00-15:00 UTC moves 1.5+ ATR one way on elevated volume, follow it for up to 6 hours.
results.why: US cash-session and ETF-related flows are the largest directional flows of the day and are worked over hours, not minutes. The losers are traders who fade the US-open move too early.
results.risk: US data releases at 13:30 UTC cause spikes that fully reverse, and the entry comes after the move.

results.name: oi_buildup_range_break
results.one_liner: Open interest builds 5%+ inside a tight 48-hour range; go with the break of that range.
results.why: Leverage added inside a narrow range means one side is wrong by construction when the range breaks and must exit in the breakout direction. The losers are the new positions that are immediately offside.
results.risk: OI builds can be hedged basis trades that never unwind; the signal is rare, so the sample will be small.

results.name: oi_confirmed_breakout
results.one_liner: Go with a new 30-bar extreme only when open interest has risen 5%+ over the same window.
results.why: Rising open interest on a breakout means new positions are being opened, and whoever opened against the move is trapped. The losers are faders who added against the breakout.
results.risk: More open interest also means more leverage to liquidate if the break fails: bigger and faster reversals.

results.name: oi_divergence_fade
results.one_liner: Fade a new 30-bar extreme that is made while open interest has dropped 5%+ over the same window.
results.why: A move made of position closing (short covering or long liquidation) has no new money behind it and tends to stall when the closing ends. The losers are breakout traders chasing a move that only reflects exits.
results.risk: OI falls in every sell-off, so the long side is knife-catching with a 2-ATR stop.

results.name: oi_reset_trend
results.one_liner: In a 50/200 trend, enter with the trend after a 24h counter-move that cut open interest by 5%+.
results.why: The counter-move has forced out the weak leveraged hands, so the trend can resume without their overhang. The losers are over-levered trend followers who were stopped at the worst price.
results.risk: A 5% drop in open interest can be the start of a regime change rather than a reset.

results.name: pullback_limit_sma
results.one_liner: In a 20/100 trend, rest a limit at the 20-bar average each bar; target the prior 20-bar extreme, stop 2 ATR beyond the average.
results.why: Buying where trend followers habitually reload, and earning the maker fee for it, is cheaper than chasing. The losers are impatient momentum traders who pay taker fees at the extreme.
results.risk: Adverse selection: fills cluster on the bars where the trend is breaking, not where it is pausing.

results.name: range_breakout_volume
results.one_liner: Close outside a tight 48-hour range on at least twice the average hourly volume: go with it.
results.why: A range break on heavy volume means the resting orders at the range edge were consumed by aggressive flow instead of absorbing it. The losers are range faders and the stops parked just outside the range.
results.risk: Volume spikes also mark stop-runs that reverse within hours; costs are large next to a 1h move.

results.name: rsi2_trend_pullback
results.one_liner: Above the 200-bar average buy a 2-bar RSI below 10 (two hard down closes), mirror below it; leave when RSI crosses 50.
results.why: Short, sharp counter-trend drops inside an established trend are mostly profit-taking and stop-runs, not new information. The losers are short-term sellers who hit bids at the low of a dip in a rising market.
results.risk: Small average win: fees and one trend-ending drop eat many wins. Very cost-sensitive.

results.name: squeeze_blowoff_fade
results.one_liner: After a 1h bar that rises 2+ ATR on 3x volume with open interest down 2%+ (shorts liquidated), sell the next open for a half retrace.
results.why: Short liquidations are forced buying at any price; once they are exhausted there is no natural buyer at the new level. The losers are the squeezed shorts and the momentum buyers who chase the spike.
results.risk: Real breakouts start exactly like this, and a short into strength has no natural ceiling on the loss beyond the stop.

results.name: trend_pullback_ma
results.one_liner: In a 50/200 trend, enter when a bar dips to the 50-bar average and closes back beyond it in the trend direction.
results.why: Under-invested trend participants use the first dip to a widely watched average to add, after early profit-takers have sold. The losers are counter-trend traders who read the dip as a reversal.
results.risk: The last pullback of every trend is the one that fails; a stop under the dip low is easily run in volatile markets.

results.name: tsmom
results.one_liner: Once a day, hold the sign of the trailing 30-day return; 4-ATR disaster stop.
results.why: Time-series momentum is the best documented futures anomaly: under-reaction to news and trend-chasing flows make last month's sign persist. The losers are contrarians and late hedgers trading against the drift.
results.risk: V-shaped reversals: the sign only flips after much of the reversal has already happened.

results.name: us_close_asia_fade
results.one_liner: At 00:00 UTC, if the last 4 hours moved 2.5+ ATR, fade half of it during the Asian morning.
results.why: Moves made in the thinnest hours of the day (late US) overshoot because little liquidity is there to absorb them. The losers are late-session momentum chasers and liquidations into a thin book.
results.risk: Weakest hypothesis in the set: thin-hour moves are sometimes the informed ones, and the sample is small.

results.name: vol_squeeze_breakout
results.one_liner: After Bollinger bands sat inside Keltner channels (a squeeze), take the first close outside the bands.
results.why: Volatility clusters and mean-reverts, so very quiet stretches end in expansion, and stops pile up on both sides of a tight range. The losers are short-volatility range traders whose stops fuel the first leg.
results.risk: The first break out of a squeeze is often a head-fake, and the mid-band stop is close.

results.name: week_range_breakout_volume
results.one_liner: Close outside a tight 7-day range while the last day's volume runs 30% above the prior week: go with it.
results.why: A week-long balance area holds a lot of inventory; when price leaves it on rising participation the side caught inside has to exit over several days. The losers are swing traders positioned for the range to hold.
results.risk: Few signals, and a false break of a weekly range costs a full 2-ATR stop.
